displayQuote: If opportunity doesn't knock, build a door

meta.title: Who really said "If opportunity doesn't knock, build a door"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Milton Berle gets the credit, but no primary source exists. The line is only documented from 1993 and is absent from Berle's own 10,000-gag book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If opportunity doesn't knock, build a door'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Milton Berle since 1993, but with no primary source and doubts from quote researchers. An honest look at a self-made-success motto.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Berle and squarely in keeping with his self-made-hustler story — but the line is only documented in print from 1993, always as a secondhand quotation, and no book, interview, or broadcast in which Berle himself said it has ever been found. Quote researcher Barry Popik notes it is “not certain when (or if) Berle ever said it,” and it is absent from Berle’s own 1989 collection of more than 10,000 jokes.

source.heading: A motto with no origin

source.excerpt: “If opportunity doesn’t knock, build a door.”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Berle, sourcing it to Arthur Pine & Julie Houston’s One Door Closes, Another Door Opens (1995, p. 109) — a motivational book quoting Berle, not Berle’s own writing.
Etymologist Barry Popik traces the earliest print appearances to 1993 — the Pine & Houston book and Robin Casey’s How to Find a Job — both already attributing it to Berle with no earlier trail.
Popik flags that the line does not appear in Berle’s own 1989 book of more than 10,000 gags, and concludes it is uncertain whether he ever said it.
source.excerptNote: The wording is unstable in circulation: many sources open with “When” rather than “If,” a hallmark of a saying passed by repetition rather than copied from a fixed text.
source.rightsNote: Because no primary source for this exact wording has ever been documented — it surfaces only as a secondhand quotation from 1993 onward — its authorship and first fixed publication cannot be established, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. If Berle did originate it, any fixed 1990s text would be modern and in copyright; if the phrasing is anonymous folk-motivational wording, there is no identifiable rights holder at all.

author.name: Milton Berle
author.heading: About Milton Berle
author.bio: Milton Berle (born Mendel Berlinger) was an American comedian and actor whose career ran from silent films and vaudeville through radio to television, where his Texaco Star Theatre made him television’s first mass-audience star and earned him the nickname “Mr. Television.” A relentless self-promoter famous for — and self-deprecating about — borrowing other comedians’ material, he became a natural magnet for punchy, self-made-success one-liners like this one.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Arthur Pine and Julie Houston, One Door Closes, Another Door Opens (New York: Delacorte Press / Dell, 1993/1995), attributed to Milton Berle; no primary source located. Citation history compiled by Barry Popik.

misattribution.heading: Credited, but never sourced
misattribution.intro: This is less a clear misattribution than an unverifiable one: the credit to Berle is everywhere, the evidence for it is nowhere.

items.why: Every popular site — BrainyQuote, Goodreads, and others — names Berle with no source. The trail dead-ends at 1993 books that merely quote him, and the line is missing from his own 1989 gag collection, per Barry Popik.

The saying circulates as both “If opportunity doesn’t knock…” and “When opportunity doesn’t knock…,” an instability typical of oral motivational lore rather than a quotation copied from a fixed, authored text.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: a genuinely good line reasonably attributed to Milton Berle, but documented only from 1993, never in his own words, and doubted by the one researcher who actually traced it — Barry Popik.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Berle
lead: The line rewards a specific kind of person: someone who clawed his way up rather than waiting to be discovered. Berle’s public story — child performer, vaudeville grinder, then the man who arguably built the door that early television walked through — makes him a frictionless host for the sentiment, which is exactly how orphan quotes find famous homes.

That fit is why it’s worth being careful. A quote that ‘sounds like’ its supposed author is the hardest kind to dislodge, because the resemblance feels like evidence. Here the resemblance is real and the evidence is not: credible attribution, unverifiable authorship.
context.pull: Berle didn’t wait for the door. Whether he wrote the line about it is another question.
